17208-the-tales-of-mother-goose-as-first:
Charles Perrault first gathered these tales in 1696, and Charles Welsh made this new translation, with an introduction by M. V. O'Shea and pictures after Gustave Dore. Cinderella and her glass slipper leads, followed by Sleeping Beauty, Little Thumb, Puss in Boots, Riquet of the Tuft, Blue Beard, The Fairy, and Little Red Riding-Hood.

The tales keep their old morals and their sharp edges: wolves, ogres, and cruel husbands sit beside kind fairies and clever cats. Welsh's plain English and Dore-based pictures suit family reading. This is a fine first Perrault for children and adults who want the classic tales close to their first French form.
24745-the-loss-of-the-kent-east-indiaman:
General Sir Duncan MacGregor wrote this account as a letter to a friend, telling how the East Indiaman Kent burned in the Bay of Biscay. The ship left the Downs bound for Bengal and China with 641 people aboard: soldiers of the 31st Regiment, their wives and children, passengers, and crew. Fire broke out at sea, and the days that followed tested every soul on board.

MacGregor, then in his nineties when he revised the tale, stresses calm courage, order amid panic, and the rescue that saved so many. The letter reads as both a sea story and a sermon on providence under fire. It remains a vivid firsthand account of one of the great ship disasters of the sailing age.
6028-opening-a-chestnut-burr:
E. P. Roe sends out his fourth venture, a simple October story, with few words of preface. He has taken well-deserved criticism from gentlemen of the caustic pen without hard feeling, and wonders they found so much to praise. How critics judge this newcomer he leaves to the future.

Roe pictures his true readers around glowing hearths in quiet homes like those he describes. He hopes the book will be welcomed for the sake of its predecessors and may make friends of its own. Letters from every class and corner of the country encouraged him. The novel offers homely warmth for autumn evenings.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-eliza-allen-s:
Eliza Allen Starr was an American writer and lecturer on art, born at Deerfield, Massachusetts, in 1824 and dead at Durand, Illinois, in 1901. Schooled at home, she traced her father's line to Dr. Comfort Starr, who settled at Cambridge in 1633. At thirteen she went to Boston, finished her studies in 1845, and opened a studio there, then moved to Brooklyn and Philadelphia and taught drawing at Natchez.

Meeting Bishop Kenrick in Philadelphia stirred a faith already in her heart, and after nine years of struggle she was received into the Catholic Church at Boston on 23 December 1854. At Chicago from 1856 she found her life's work, writing books and illustrating them with her own pencil, lecturing across the United States, and giving ten lectures a year at home. Her books include Songs of a Lifetime, Patron Saints, Pilgrims and Shrines, and a life of Isabella of Castile.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-curr:
Joseph Curr was an English priest remembered as a controversialist and a martyr of charity. Born at Sheffield late in the eighteenth century, he studied at Crook Hall and Ushaw College and served missions in Manchester, where he debated the Protestant Bible Association. After a retreat at La Trappe in France, he worked at Callaly, Blackburn, and Whitby.

In 1847, when typhus struck Leeds and priests were scarce, Curr volunteered for the stricken city and died of the fever on 29 June. His writings include a Sunday-school aid, translations from Liguori and Bourdaloue, and Familiar Instructions in Catholic Faith and Morality. Sermons and controversial pamphlets also survive.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-finbarr:
Finbarr, bishop and patron of Cork, evangelized Munster's towns before settling where Cork city now stands. Born near Bandon about 550, son of Amergin, he preached at Gowran, Coolcashin, and Aghaboe, founded a school at Eirce, and dwelt for years as a hermit at Gougane Barra. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Cloyne to 25 September 623.

He was buried in the cathedral he built on the site of Cork, and honoured also at Dornoch and Barra in Scotland. A modern replica of Cormac's chapel now stands at Gougane Barra in his honour. Five Irish saints share his name, and the entry keeps this Finbarr, Lochan or Barr, distinct. The portrait is brief: preacher, school founder, hermit, and city patron in one life.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-HarrisLarryLSee:
Tom Belden wrote a viewpoint piece for the Dallas Morning News on November 22, 1977. His subject was the people who gather at Dealey Plaza. On the eve of the fourteenth anniversary of the assassination, doubters were assembling at the grassy knoll, the slope at the center of so many theories.

Anniversaries turned the plaza into a meeting place for the unconvinced. Belden, writing in the city's own paper, watched his hometown's wound become a yearly convention. The piece preserves how Dallas itself regarded the pilgrims who kept returning to the scene.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-VanderKerr_Van_: Chapter III of a book on the assassination looks at how Dallas television and radio covered the killing on Friday, November 22, 1963. Local stations were the first to carry the news, often with confused early reports. The chapter studies their broadcasts as both journalism and historical record. For media history, few days show live local coverage under pressure as clearly as that Friday in Dallas.
opening-a-chestnut-burr:
Edward Payson Roe called this novel, his fourth book, a simple October story, and sent it out hoping it would enter homes the way his earlier ones had. In his preface he pictures readers around a glowing hearth in quiet houses, and says the book was really written for them. Its hero, he hints in verse, is like a great ship caught halfway across the sea with its stores run out.

Roe promises that the book's purpose will become clear as it is read, and that its incidents and characters are mainly imagined. The subject he writes on, the preface says, cannot be separated from happiness in this world or the next. Victorian readers made Roe one of the most popular novelists of his day.
the-tales-of-mother-goose-as-first-colle: Charles Welsh translated Charles Perrault's Tales of Mother Goose for D. C. Heath, working from Perrault's first collection of 1696, with an introduction by M. V. O'Shea and pictures after Gustave Doré. Merely the front pages and contents are present in this record, so none of the fairy tales themselves can be read here. The contents name eight stories, among them Cinderella, Sleeping Beauty, Puss in Boots, Blue Beard, and Little Red Riding-Hood. The list alone shows the core of the Mother Goose collection that shaped later fairy-tale books.
